This page goes with **Chapter 34, Serialism** of Robert Hutchinson's open textbook
[*Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom*](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/Serialism.html). Read each section there first.
It uses the pitch-class integers of [Chapter 33](set-theory.qmd): C = 0, T = 10, E = 11.

## 34.1 The twelve-tone row

In twelve-tone technique (Schoenberg, Webern and Berg, the book says) a piece is built from one ordering of all twelve pitch classes, the **row**.
Every pitch class appears once, and the order stays fixed; the row may be turned into other forms and moved to other pitch levels. Immediate
repeats, trills and tremolos are allowed to bend the "no repeated note" rule. The book's example is Schoenberg's Suite for Piano, Op. 25
([find the score on IMSLP](https://imslp.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Schoenberg+Suite+Op.25), [listen](https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=Schoenberg+Suite+for+Piano+Op.25)).
The row it uses is the page's first preset below (written from memory, unchecked against the score).

## 34.2 Four forms and their numbers

| Form | What it is | Numbered by |
|---|---|---|
| **P** (prime) | the row itself | its first note |
| **I** (inversion) | every interval turned upside down | its first note |
| **R** (retrograde) | P backwards | its last note |
| **RI** (retrograde inversion) | I backwards | its last note |

So P<sub>4</sub> starts on E, and R<sub>4</sub> is P<sub>4</sub> reversed, which ends on E. Each form can start on any of the twelve notes, giving 48 forms in all.

## 34.3 The matrix

A **twelve-tone matrix** lays all 48 forms in a 12&times;12 grid. The top row is P; the left column is I; the diagonal from top left is all one note.
Each row is a P form (read right to left it is R); each column is an I form (read bottom to top it is RI).
Build one below, then click a label around the edge to hear and see that form. The staff shows the form as quarter notes.

::: {.pt data-pt="matrix"}
:::

Things to look for: the hexachord set classes (a row's two halves are complements, and some rows have the same class in both halves);
the interval list (which interval never appears?). Try the "all-interval" preset against the chromatic scale.

## 34.4 Naming a form

Compare the first few intervals. If the opening is up a minor third and down a major second, only one form of the row begins that way.
P and I are named by the first note, so find the form, then read its first note; for R and RI read the last note. The matrix tool's
"Which form is this series?" box does the lookup for you.

## Practice

Take the row E F G D&flat; G&flat; E&flat; A&flat; D B C A B&flat; = 4 5 7 1 6 3 8 2 11 0 9 10.

1. Write I<sub>9</sub>.
2. Write R<sub>5</sub>.
3. Is 11 2 10 6 3 4 0 9 5 1 7 8 a form of this row?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers

1. I<sub>9</sub> = 9 8 6 0 7 10 5 11 2 1 4 3.
2. R<sub>5</sub> = P<sub>5</sub> backwards = 11 10 1 0 3 9 4 7 2 8 6 5 (it ends on 5).
3. No: it is not one of the 48 forms (the tool says so).
:::

## Non-twelve-tone serialism

The chapter ends by noting that the idea of fixed series can be applied to other things than pitch, such as rhythm or dynamics, or to series of fewer
than twelve elements. Composers often named for this (Boulez, Babbitt, Messiaen) are from memory and unverified here.
